question: Please introduce yourself.
questionHi: कृपया अपना परिचय दें।
checking: Relevance — do you connect your background to teaching?
keyPoints: Name, place, family background in one line
Educational qualifications (graduation, D.El.Ed./B.Ed., CTET/TET)
Teaching experience or exposure to children
Why primary teaching — a genuine reason
One strength relevant to PRT role
commonMistakes: Reciting the whole biodata including marks of Class 10
Only personal details with no link to teaching
answerStructure: Close with what you bring to KVS
sampleAnswer: Good morning, respected members of the board. I am Priya Sharma from Lucknow. I completed my graduation in Science and my D.El.Ed., and I have qualified CTET Paper I. For the last two years I have taught Classes 2 and 3 at a private school, where I worked especially on foundational reading with slow readers. I chose primary teaching because the first eight years shape a child's attitude to learning, and I enjoy making concepts concrete through activities and stories. I believe my patience, planning habit and interest in FLN would help me contribute to a Kendriya Vidyalaya.
followUps: You mentioned working with slow readers — what exactly did you do?
What is one thing about yourself that is not on your résumé?
How has your family supported your decision to become a teacher?

question: Why do you want to join Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan?
questionHi: आप केंद्रीय विद्यालय संगठन में क्यों शामिल होना चाहती हैं?
checking: Knowledge of KVS's mission and features
Genuine alignment of values, not only job security
Awareness of the PRT role in a KV
keyPoints: KVS mission: uniform education for children of transferable Central Govt employees
CBSE-affiliated, NCERT curriculum, common pan-India pattern
Culture of co-scholastic activities, ZIET-based professional development
PM SHRI / NEP implementation leadership among government schools
Personal fit: diverse classrooms, structured system, growth as a professional
commonMistakes: Saying only 'government job' or 'salary and security'
Quoting outdated numbers of KVs confidently
answerStructure: State KVS's unique mission in one line
Two specific features you admire (curriculum uniformity, co-scholastic culture, teacher training)
sampleAnswer: KVS was created so that children of transferable Central Government employees get the same quality of education anywhere in India — I find that mission meaningful because a child should never suffer academically because of a parent's posting. KVs follow NCERT and CBSE with a strong co-scholastic culture and structured in-service training through ZIETs, and many KVs are now PM SHRI schools leading NEP 2020 implementation. As a teacher who likes structured planning and diverse classrooms, I feel I can grow here while contributing to foundational learning.
followUps: What do you know about the motto of KVS?
How is teaching in a KV different from a state government school?
Would you be comfortable with transfer to another state?

question: Why should we select you as a PRT over other candidates?
questionHi: हम आपको अन्य अभ्यर्थियों की तुलना में PRT के रूप में क्यों चुनें?
checking: Fit with PRT competencies: patience, FLN skills, activity-based teaching, multi-subject ability
keyPoints: Two or three concrete strengths with examples
Multi-subject readiness (PRTs teach all subjects)
Understanding of foundational stage pedagogy
Attitude: learner, team player, adaptable to transfers
sampleAnswer: I cannot speak for other candidates, but I can share what I bring. First, I am strong in foundational literacy — in my last school I used a structured phonics-plus-storytelling approach and the reading level of my Class 2 group improved measurably over one year. Second, I plan every lesson around a concrete activity, because children in the concrete operational stage learn by doing. Third, I am comfortable teaching all subjects at the primary level, and I adapt quickly to new places, which matters in KVS. I am a continuous learner and would be committed to the KV community.
followUps: Give one example where your planning did not work. What did you change?
Which subject do you find hardest to teach and why?

question: How would you plan and teach a lesson on 'Water' to Class 3?
questionHi: आप कक्षा 3 के लिए 'पानी' विषय पर पाठ की योजना और शिक्षण कैसे करेंगी?
checking: Use of prior knowledge, activities and TLM
keyPoints: Learning outcomes first (NCERT LOs for Class 3 EVS)
Set induction with a question or story about daily water use
Hands-on activity: sources of water, states of water, clean vs dirty water experiment
Group work and discussion; local context (taps, hand-pumps, rivers)
Values: conservation, hygiene
Formative assessment: drawing, oral questions, exit ticket
commonMistakes: No mention of learning outcomes or assessment
sampleAnswer: I would begin with the NCERT learning outcome — children identify sources and uses of water and the need to conserve it. For set induction I would ask 'What did you do with water this morning?' and list answers on the board. Then two activities: first, in groups children sort picture cards into sources of water — river, well, hand-pump, tap, rain; second, a simple demonstration of filtering muddy water through cloth to discuss clean water and hygiene. We would read a short story or poem about rain to integrate language, and count buckets used at home for a numeracy link. I would close with a 'water promise' for conservation, and assess through oral questions and a drawing of two sources of water in their area. For follow-up, children would observe water use at home for a day.
followUps: How would you handle a child who says water comes only from the tap?
What TLM would you prepare if the school has no lab?

question: What is the importance of Piaget's theory for a primary teacher?
questionHi: प्राथमिक शिक्षक के लिए पियाजे के सिद्धांत का क्या महत्व है?
checking: Ability to convert theory into classroom practice
keyPoints: Pre-operational (2–7) and concrete operational (7–11) cover primary classes
Children learn through concrete objects, manipulation, hands-on experience
Egocentrism, conservation, reversibility — implications
Readiness: do not teach abstract concepts before readiness
Discovery/active learning; peer interaction
commonMistakes: Only listing stage names and ages
Not giving a single classroom example
answerStructure: Which stages primary children are in
sampleAnswer: Piaget showed that children actively construct knowledge and think qualitatively differently at different stages. Children in Classes 1–2 are largely pre-operational and Classes 3–5 concrete operational. So, first, I teach with concrete materials — counters, ganit mala, real objects — before symbols. Second, since young children struggle with conservation and reversibility, I use pouring and regrouping activities in maths rather than telling rules. Third, I let children explore and discover, because assimilation and accommodation happen through experience. One caution: Piaget under-estimated the role of social interaction and culture, which Vygotsky emphasised, so I also use peer learning and scaffolding.
followUps: Can you give an example of a conservation task?
How does Vygotsky differ from Piaget?

question: How will you manage a class of 40 students of Class 1 who are restless and noisy?
questionHi: कक्षा 1 के 40 बेचैन और शोर करने वाले बच्चों की कक्षा को आप कैसे संभालेंगी?
keyPoints: Establish simple routines and signals (clap pattern, song, hand signal)
Short activity cycles — 10–12 minute attention span
Movement and action songs; energy release
Seating in small groups; peer buddies
Positive reinforcement and clear expectations co-created with children
Address root causes — hunger, boredom, unclear instructions
sampleAnswer: For six-year-olds, noise usually means unmet needs — boredom, sitting too long or unclear instructions — so my first tool is prevention. I would set two or three simple class rules with pictures, use a consistent attention signal like a clap pattern or a short song, and change activity every 10–12 minutes with movement breaks and action songs. I would seat children in small groups with a peer buddy and give responsibilities like line leader. During the class I would use proximity, a quiet voice and specific praise — 'Group 2 is ready with their books' — rather than shouting. Consistency over the first few weeks is what makes it work.
followUps: What will you do if one particular child continues to disturb despite routines?
How would you involve parents?

question: A child with hearing impairment joins your Class 4. How will you include her in your teaching?
questionHi: कक्षा 4 में एक श्रवण-बाधित बच्ची आती है। आप उसे अपने शिक्षण में कैसे शामिल करेंगी?
checking: Knowledge of RPwD Act and inclusive practices
Collaboration with special educator and parents
keyPoints: Front seating facing the teacher; face the class while speaking; good lighting
Visual supports — pictures, written instructions, captions; gestures and basic Indian Sign Language
Peer buddy system; check understanding often
Coordinate with special educator/resource teacher and parents; hearing aid support
Sensitise class; avoid isolation; assessment accommodations
Legal basis: RPwD Act 2016, NEP 2020 Chapter 6
commonMistakes: Suggesting she be sent to a special school
answerStructure: Attitude and legal frame in one line
sampleAnswer: Inclusion is her right under the RPwD Act 2016 and my responsibility, so I would start by learning from her parents and the special educator what she hears and whether she uses a hearing aid. In class I would seat her at the front facing me, always speak while facing the class, and pair every oral instruction with a visual — written keywords, pictures, gestures — and learn some basic Indian Sign Language signs with the whole class so that it becomes a class skill, not a label. I would give her a peer buddy, check understanding through quick written or drawn responses, and allow accommodations in assessment such as written instead of oral tasks. I would keep in touch with the resource teacher and parents regularly.
followUps: How would you handle classmates who tease her?
What accommodations would you give in a class test?
source: RPwD Act 2016; Samagra Shiksha inclusive education

question: What are the key features of NEP 2020 relevant to a primary teacher?
questionHi: NEP 2020 की प्राथमिक शिक्षक के लिए प्रासंगिक प्रमुख विशेषताएँ क्या हैं?
keyPoints: 5+3+3+4 structure; Foundational (3–8) and Preparatory (8–11) stages
FLN as urgent national mission (NIPUN Bharat)
Mother tongue/home language as medium till at least Grade 5
Play-, activity-, discovery-based and experiential learning; no hard separation of curricular/co-curricular
Competency-based education and reduced curriculum load
Assessment reform: Holistic Progress Card, PARAKH, formative 360°
Teacher: 50 hours CPD per year; 4-year ITEP
commonMistakes: Listing higher-education points (4-year UG) irrelevant to PRT
sampleAnswer: For a primary teacher the most important shifts in NEP 2020 are: first, the 5+3+3+4 structure — I would be teaching in the Foundational Stage, ages 3 to 8, and the Preparatory Stage, ages 8 to 11, where play-based and activity-based pedagogy is recommended. Second, foundational literacy and numeracy is declared an urgent national mission, implemented through NIPUN Bharat with targets by Grade 3. Third, mother tongue or home language as medium wherever possible till at least Grade 5, and a multilingual approach. Fourth, competency-based learning with reduced content load and experiential methods. Fifth, assessment reform — the Holistic Progress Card, a 360-degree formative assessment, and PARAKH as the national assessment centre. Finally, teachers must do at least 50 hours of continuous professional development every year, which I welcome.
followUps: What is the Holistic Progress Card?
How would you implement mother-tongue teaching in a KV where children come from many states?

question: What is NIPUN Bharat and how would you achieve its goals in your classroom?
questionHi: निपुण भारत क्या है और आप अपनी कक्षा में इसके लक्ष्य कैसे प्राप्त करेंगी?
keyPoints: Launched 5 July 2021 under Samagra Shiksha; goal — FLN for every child by end of Grade 3 (target 2026-27)
Lakshya (goals) for Balvatika to Grade 3; three developmental goals
Literacy: oral language, phonological awareness, decoding, vocabulary, reading fluency, comprehension, writing
Numeracy: number sense, operations, shapes, measurement, patterns, data
Strategies: print-rich class, read-alouds, structured phonics with meaning, TLM, ganit mala, games
Regular tracking — oral reading fluency, simple numeracy checks; remedial groups
commonMistakes: Confusing NIPUN with a scheme for higher classes
sampleAnswer: NIPUN Bharat was launched in July 2021 under Samagra Shiksha to ensure every child achieves foundational literacy and numeracy by the end of Grade 3. It gives grade-wise Lakshyas from Balvatika to Class 3. In my classroom, for literacy I would create a print-rich environment, do daily read-alouds and shared reading, build phonological awareness through rhymes and sound games, teach decoding of aksharas with meaning-based texts, and give daily time for children's own writing and drawing. For numeracy I would build number sense with concrete materials like ganit mala and bundles-and-sticks, use games for operations, and connect to daily life. I would track oral reading fluency and simple numeracy checks every few weeks and run small remedial groups for children who need more support.
followUps: What is the difference between phonological awareness and phonics?
How would you teach a child who cannot recognise numbers 1–9 in Class 2?

question: How would you handle a child who is consistently weak in mathematics?
questionHi: गणित में लगातार कमजोर बच्चे को आप कैसे संभालेंगी?
keyPoints: Diagnose the specific gap (place value? operations? language of word problems?)
Go back to concrete materials, then pictures, then symbols (CPA)
Small steps, frequent success, specific praise; remove maths anxiety
Peer tutoring and games; connect to daily life (shopping, cricket scores)
Short daily remedial slot; track progress; involve parents with simple home activities
Check for learning difficulties like dyscalculia if it persists
sampleAnswer: I would first find out exactly where the difficulty lies — for example, a child who fails in subtraction may actually be confused about place value. So I would do a short diagnostic with concrete tasks. Then I would re-teach from concrete to pictorial to abstract: bundles of sticks and ganit mala before written algorithms. I would break tasks into small steps so the child experiences success daily and praise the effort specifically to reduce maths anxiety. I would pair the child with a supportive peer, use games and real-life contexts like shopping, and give parents one simple ten-minute home activity. I would track progress every two weeks, and if the difficulty persists despite this, I would discuss with the counsellor or special educator to screen for a learning difficulty such as dyscalculia.
followUps: What specific activities would you use to improve place value understanding?
How would you keep the rest of the class engaged while you work with this child?

question: How would you handle a gifted child who finishes work quickly and gets bored?
questionHi: एक प्रतिभाशाली बच्चा जो काम जल्दी पूरा कर लेता है और ऊब जाता है, उसे आप कैसे संभालेंगी?
checking: Understanding enrichment vs. more of the same
Avoiding using the child only as a helper
keyPoints: Enrichment and extension tasks — open-ended problems, projects, higher-order questions (Bloom)
Choice and autonomy; independent reading corner
Leadership roles in group work, but not permanently as 'teacher's helper'
Compacting curriculum; challenge cards
Attend to social-emotional needs; avoid isolation or arrogance
commonMistakes: Giving more of the same worksheets
Making the child a permanent monitor
Ignoring the child because 'he is fine'
sampleAnswer: A gifted child needs depth and challenge, not more of the same work. I would prepare extension tasks in advance — open-ended problems, 'what if' questions, a small research project or a challenge card box. I would give her choice and autonomy, for example a reading corner or a creative task linked to the lesson. She can occasionally lead a group, but I would avoid making her a permanent helper, because she deserves to learn too. I would also watch her social-emotional side, so that she stays connected with peers and does not become isolated or over-confident, and keep parents informed about enrichment they can support at home.
followUps: Give an example of an open-ended maths task for Class 3.
How would you identify giftedness without a formal test?

question: A Class 5 student is aggressive, hits classmates and does not respond to warnings. What will you do?
questionHi: कक्षा 5 का एक छात्र आक्रामक है, सहपाठियों को मारता है और चेतावनी पर प्रतिक्रिया नहीं देता। आप क्या करेंगी?
checking: Systematic plan with school counsellor and parents
keyPoints: Ensure safety of others immediately; calm, non-confrontational intervention
Private conversation; listen; identify triggers (home issues, bullying, learning frustration)
Behaviour plan: clear expectations, consistent consequences, teaching alternatives (words instead of hitting), self-regulation strategies
Reinforce positive behaviour; give responsibility
Involve parents, school counsellor; refer if needed
Never corporal punishment or humiliation (RTE Sec. 17, JJ Act)
commonMistakes: Suggesting punishment or suspension as first step
sampleAnswer: My first duty is safety, so I would calmly separate the children and de-escalate without shouting or physical force. Later I would talk with the child privately and listen — aggression at this age is usually communication of something else: trouble at home, being bullied, or frustration with learning. I would then make a simple behaviour plan with him: clear expectations, consistent and logical consequences, and teaching alternatives — using words, a cool-down corner, a signal to me when he feels angry. I would notice and reinforce every positive step and give him a responsibility that builds self-worth. I would involve the parents as partners and the school counsellor, and refer for professional help if it continues. At no point would I use corporal punishment or humiliation, which are illegal and make aggression worse.
followUps: What if the parents deny there is any problem?
How would you protect the child who was hit, emotionally?
source: RTE Act Sec. 17; NCPCR positive discipline guidelines

question: A parent angrily complains that you are biased against their child. How will you respond?
questionHi: एक अभिभावक गुस्से में शिकायत करता है कि आप उनके बच्चे के प्रति पक्षपाती हैं। आप कैसे प्रतिक्रिया देंगी?
keyPoints: Stay calm; do not argue; take the conversation to a private setting
Listen fully; acknowledge feelings
Share objective evidence — work samples, records, observations
Agree on a joint plan with follow-up date
Inform Principal if needed; maintain records
sampleAnswer: I would stay calm and invite the parent to sit privately, because a parent's anger usually comes from worry about their child. I would listen completely without interrupting and acknowledge their feeling. Then I would share objective evidence — the child's notebooks, my observation notes, assessment records — and explain my approach. I would ask what they have observed at home, and together we would agree on two or three specific steps and a date to review. If the parent remains dissatisfied, I would involve the Principal transparently. Keeping good records and regular positive communication with all parents prevents most such situations.
followUps: How do you communicate proactively with parents?
What if the complaint has some truth in it?

question: How would you use ICT in a primary classroom without letting it replace real experiences?
questionHi: प्राथमिक कक्षा में आप ICT का उपयोग वास्तविक अनुभवों को प्रतिस्थापित किए बिना कैसे करेंगी?
checking: Balanced view — technology as a tool
Knowledge of platforms: DIKSHA, PM eVIDYA, e-Pathshala, NISHTHA
keyPoints: Purpose first: use ICT where it adds value — visualisation, audio for languages, virtual field trips
DIKSHA QR-coded content, e-Pathshala, PM eVIDYA channels; NROER/OER
Blend: concrete activity first, digital to consolidate
Limited screen time for young children; teacher-mediated
ICT for teacher's own work — assessment records, TLM creation, CPD via NISHTHA on DIKSHA
Digital safety and equity — not all homes have devices
sampleAnswer: For me technology is a tool, so I ask first whether it adds value. In a primary class it helps to visualise things children cannot see — the water cycle animation, a virtual visit to a farm, or native-speaker audio for English pronunciation. I would use DIKSHA content through QR codes in NCERT books, e-Pathshala and PM eVIDYA resources. But I would always start with concrete experience — actual seeds, actual measuring — and use the digital piece to consolidate, keeping screen time short and teacher-mediated for young children. I would also use ICT for my own work: recording formative assessment, preparing TLM, and doing NISHTHA courses for my professional development. And I would be mindful of digital safety and of children who do not have devices at home.
followUps: What is DIKSHA?
How would you conduct classes if schools shift online again?

question: Why is EVS taught as an integrated subject in Classes 3–5 and how does that change your teaching?
questionHi: कक्षा 3–5 में EVS को एकीकृत विषय के रूप में क्यों पढ़ाया जाता है और इससे आपका शिक्षण कैसे बदलता है?
keyPoints: NCF 2005: young children do not see the world in subject compartments
EVS integrates science, social studies and environmental education around six themes (family & friends, food, shelter, water, travel, things we make and do)
Start from child's own experience and local environment; observation, exploration, discussion
Values: sensitivity, equity, sustainability
Classes 1–2: EVS integrated into language and maths
commonMistakes: Not mentioning themes or child's experience
sampleAnswer: NCF 2005 recommended integrated EVS because a young child experiences the world as a whole — a visit to a market is at once science, social studies and language. So NCERT organises EVS around themes like family and friends, food, shelter, water, travel and things we make and do. This changes my teaching: I start from what children already know, take them outdoors to observe plants, shops or water sources, use interviews with family members, and let children discuss and question rather than memorise. It also carries values — sensitivity to diversity, gender equality and care for the environment — which I bring in through discussion and reflection.
followUps: Give an activity for the theme 'Food' in Class 4.
How would you assess EVS beyond written tests?

question: How would you introduce the concept of fractions to Class 4 students?
questionHi: आप कक्षा 4 के छात्रों को भिन्न की अवधारणा कैसे प्रस्तुत करेंगी?
keyPoints: Start with fair sharing — roti, chocolate bar, paper folding
Equal parts emphasis; part-whole language before symbols
Fraction strips/circles; shading; number line later
Address misconceptions (bigger denominator = bigger fraction)
Connect to daily life — half, quarter of an hour, half litre
sampleAnswer: I would start with a story of sharing a roti between two friends and ask how to share fairly, emphasising equal parts. Children would fold paper strips and circles into halves and quarters, colouring parts and using words like 'one out of two equal parts' before I introduce the symbol ½. Next they would make fraction strips and compare — which is bigger, one-third or one-half — to confront the common misconception that a bigger bottom number means a bigger fraction. Only then would I introduce the terms numerator and denominator and later the number line. Throughout I would connect to daily life — half an hour, quarter kilo.
followUps: A child says 1/3 is bigger than 1/2 because 3 is bigger than 2. How do you respond?
How would you assess understanding of fractions?

question: Most children in your class speak Hindi at home. How will you teach them English?
questionHi: आपकी कक्षा के अधिकांश बच्चे घर पर हिंदी बोलते हैं। आप उन्हें अंग्रेजी कैसे सिखाएँगी?
checking: Using home language as resource, not obstacle
Focus on listening and speaking first
keyPoints: Comprehensible input: rhymes, stories, TPR (Total Physical Response), picture talk
Listening-speaking before reading-writing; low-anxiety environment
Use Hindi as a bridge (translanguaging), not banned
Print-rich English environment; labels; big books; songs
Meaningful communication tasks rather than grammar drills
NEP 2020 multilingualism
sampleAnswer: Children learn a second language the way they learned the first — by hearing a lot of meaningful language and being allowed to speak without fear. So I would flood the class with English rhymes, action songs, TPR commands like 'stand up, touch your nose', and picture stories, focusing on listening and speaking first. I would not ban Hindi; I would use it as a bridge to explain and then return to English, following NEP 2020's multilingual approach. The class would be print-rich with labels and big books, and I would give simple communicative tasks — greeting, describing a picture — rather than grammar drills. Reading and writing would follow gradually from the words children already know orally.
followUps: What is TPR? Give an example.
How would you handle a child too shy to speak English?
source: NCF 2005 Position Paper on English; NEP 2020

question: कक्षा 1 के बच्चों को हिंदी पढ़ना सिखाने की आपकी विधि क्या होगी?
questionHi: कक्षा 1 के बच्चों को हिंदी पढ़ना सिखाने की आपकी विधि क्या होगी?
checking: Knowledge of varna/akshara and matra progression
keyPoints: मौखिक भाषा विकास पहले — कहानी, कविता, बातचीत
अक्षर-ध्वनि संबंध सिखाना, पर अर्थपूर्ण शब्दों/वाक्यों के साथ (संतुलित उपागम)
बिना मात्रा शब्द → मात्राएँ क्रम से
चित्र-पठन, बड़ी किताबें, कक्षा में लिखित सामग्री
बच्चों का स्वयं लेखन/चित्र; पढ़ने का आनंद
निपुण भारत के लक्ष्य
sampleAnswer: मैं मौखिक भाषा से शुरू करूँगी — रोज़ कहानी, कविता और बातचीत, ताकि बच्चों का शब्द-भंडार और ध्वनि-जागरूकता बढ़े। फिर संतुलित उपागम से अक्षर-ध्वनि संबंध सिखाऊँगी — पहले बच्चों के परिचित नाम और वस्तुओं के शब्दों से अक्षर पहचान, बिना मात्रा वाले शब्दों (जैसे कमल, नमक) से शुरू करके फिर आ, इ, ई की मात्राएँ क्रम से। कक्षा में चित्र-कथाएँ, बड़ी किताबें और लिखित सामग्री होगी और हर दिन बच्चे स्वयं कुछ लिखेंगे या चित्र बनाकर बताएँगे। निपुण भारत के लक्ष्यों के अनुसार मैं समय-समय पर पठन-प्रवाह जाँचकर आवश्यक सहयोग दूँगी।
followUps: ध्वनि-जागरूकता बढ़ाने की एक गतिविधि बताइए।
जो बच्चा मात्राएँ मिलाकर नहीं पढ़ पाता, उसके लिए क्या करेंगी?

question: What do you know about Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan — its motto, mission and structure?
questionHi: केंद्रीय विद्यालय संगठन — इसके ध्येय वाक्य, मिशन और संरचना के बारे में आप क्या जानती हैं?
checking: Whether you checked the official website recently
keyPoints: Autonomous body under Ministry of Education; Minister of Education is Chairman
Started 1963 (Central Schools scheme approved 1962); registered society 1965
Motto: 'तत्त्वं पूषन् अपावृणु' from Ishavasya Upanishad
Mission: uniform education for children of transferable Central Govt employees, excellence, national integration
CBSE-affiliated, NCERT curriculum; Regional Offices; ZIETs for training; Headquarters New Delhi
Quote latest number of KVs from official site (do not guess)
commonMistakes: Not knowing it is under Ministry of Education
sampleAnswer: KVS is an autonomous body under the Ministry of Education, and the Union Education Minister is its Chairman. The Central Schools scheme was approved in 1962, schools started in 1963, and the Sangathan was registered as a society in 1965. Its motto, 'Tattvam Pūṣan Apāvṛṇu', from the Ishavasya Upanishad, means 'O Nourisher, uncover the truth'. Its mission is to provide uniform, quality education to children of transferable Central Government employees, to pursue excellence, and to promote national integration. KVs are CBSE-affiliated and follow NCERT; the organisation works through regional offices and ZIETs for teacher training, with headquarters in New Delhi. The exact number of KVs changes as new ones are sanctioned, so I checked the official website today for the latest figure.

question: During your class you notice a child has bruises and seems fearful. What will you do?
questionHi: कक्षा के दौरान आप देखती हैं कि एक बच्चे के शरीर पर चोट के निशान हैं और वह भयभीत दिखता है। आप क्या करेंगी?
checking: Child protection awareness (POCSO, JJ Act, school CP policy)
keyPoints: Do not ignore; do not interrogate the child or make promises
Speak gently, privately; ensure the child feels safe
Document observations factually
Report immediately to Principal / school child-protection committee as per KVS/CBSE guidelines
Legal duty: POCSO Act 2012 mandatory reporting (Sec. 19–21); Childline 1098
Maintain confidentiality; continue support
sampleAnswer: I would take it seriously and never assume it is only a family matter. I would speak to the child gently and privately to make him feel safe, without interrogating or promising things I cannot control. I would note down what I observed factually — date, marks, behaviour. I would report it the same day to the Principal and the school's child protection committee, because under the POCSO Act reporting is mandatory and the school has a defined procedure; if needed, Childline 1098 can be contacted. I would maintain confidentiality, not confront parents on my own, and keep supporting the child in class so that school remains a safe place for him.
